title: ADA Report Finds Dentists Less Busy and Less Confident as Costs Outpace Payments
html:
Two in five dentists said they were not busy enough and could have treated more patients in the third quarter of 2026, up from about one-quarter the previous quarter, according to the American Dental Association Health Policy Institute’s quarterly report on the U.S. dental economy, released in October.

Dentists’ economic confidence fell after edging up earlier in the year, with lower ratings for their own practices, the dental care sector, and the U.S. economy. More dentists were still confident (40.9%) than skeptical (36.9%) about the dental sector. Skeptics most often cited low reimbursement and insurance pressures, rising costs, and patients not prioritizing dental care.

The institute described a continuing “fiscal squeeze” inside practices. From January through August, reimbursement averaged across all payers rose 1.5% while overall inflation reached 2.3%. Since January 2021, reimbursement has risen 19% against 27% inflation, while prices for dental equipment and supplies rose 23% and hourly earnings of dental office staff rose 21%.

Consumer spending on dental care was down 2.4% for the year through August. The institute said the decline may reflect fewer patients visiting the dentist, fewer patients accepting treatment plans, and lower reimbursement. Appointment wait times also fell.

Staffing remained tight. About one-third of dentists were recruiting dental hygienists during the quarter, and most of them described it as very or extremely challenging. Only two in five dentists recruiting in the prior three months filled the open hygiene position, compared with about two-thirds of those recruiting dental assistants, and one in five practices reported hygienist positions open for more than six months.

The institute said the combination of stalling patient spending, economic uncertainty, lower busyness, persistent staffing shortages, and the squeeze on practice finances points to a more sluggish dental economy, and that it will watch whether conditions rebound in the fourth quarter. The quarterly report draws on the institute’s dentist panel and on federal economic data.

Sources:
ADA Health Policy Institute, “The State of the U.S. Dental Economy: 3rd Quarter 2026 Update,” October 2026: ada.org/state_us_dental_economy_q32026.pdf
